does not require regular replacements [51, 52]. Fresh vegetables can be stored for extended lengths of time due to the 
increased barrier properties of the  TiO2-containing active films. Fruits coated with active  TiO2 coatings lost less weight and 
decayed at a slower rate than uncoated pepper and tomato fruits, keeping superior quality throughout postharvest [53]. 
 TiO2 is a great option for a functional nanofiller that improves the performance of active food packaging films because 
of its low toxicity, economy, stability, and outstanding biocompatibility. In addition to acting as a crosslinking agent to 
enhance the film’s mechanical, water resistance, and gas barrier qualities, the addition of  TiO2 may give the active film 
antibacterial qualities. Nonetheless, the impact of  TiO2 on the characteristics of the active film is multifaceted; for instance, 
the influence of  TiO2 on the mechanical and water vapor barrier qualities of the active film is linked not only to the  TiO2 
concentration but also to the kind of film matrix and their interplay. Expanding the potential uses of  TiO2 through surface 
modification is necessary for the usage and commercialization of the functional packaging film added with  TiO2. This 
will enable  TiO2 to have photocatalytic activity under visible light, antibacterial properties, and an ability to scavenge 
ethylene even under normal storage circumstances of packaged foods like fresh fruits.  TiO2-added functional films are 
expected to be used in active food packaging applications because the addition of  TiO2 has increased the active film’s/
coating’s efficiency for food preservation. Additionally, the degree of  TiO2 movement from the active film to the food is 
negligible, and its safety has been established [54].

Nanocellulose is produced by the breakdown of cellulose fibres. The intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonds 
in cellulose make them insoluble in solvents, giving them high tensile and mechanical strength. Thus, nanocellulose 
when combined with other materials increases the thermal, mechanical, and barrier properties of the nanocompos-
ite. The formation of hydrogen bonds with the biopolymer results in a dense network with a very small pore size. This 
makes nanocellulose impermeable to gases and moisture [63]. A notable work by Bideau et al. (2018) [76] showed that 
paperboard coated with TEMPO oxidised cellulose nanofibers and polypyrrole, significantly increased the mechanical 
properties of the paperboard, which can be attributed to the presence of carboxyl group and hydrogen bonds in the 
cellulose nanofibers. Another piece of research conducted by Koppolu and colleagues showed the development of a 
nanocellulose reinforced with PLA on a paperboard. It showed a notable decrease in water vapour permeation rate by 
23% and oxygen transmission rate by 98% as compared with only PLA-coated paperboard [77].

preservation and packaging: a review

Ritesh Pattnaik1 · Sandeep Kumar Panda1 · Soumyadeep Biswas1 · Sayanti De1 · Subhra Satahrada1 · Subrat Kumar1

Abstract
Nanomaterials play a pivotal role in food preservation and its safety, offering ingenious solutions for sustainable food 
packaging. Nanomaterials enable the creation of packaging materials having unique functional properties. It not only 
extends the shelf life of the foods by releasing preservatives but also enhances food safety by preventing microbial 
contamination or food spoilage. In this review, we aim to provide an overview of the various applications of nanotech-
nology in food packaging, highlighting its key advantages. We also delve into the safety considerations and regulatory 
issues involved in developing nanotechnology-based food packaging materials. Additionally, advancements in the field 
of nanotechnology-based packaging have the potential to create safer, more sustainable, and high-quality packaging 
with greater functionality that delivers essential benefits to manufacturers and consumers.

Keywords  Food preservation · Food safety · Shelf life · Sustainable food packaging · Nanocomposites

1  Introduction

Over the years, food industries have faced many challenges, especially regarding ensuring food safety and food preser-
vation during storage and distribution. Throughout history, humans have strived to find effective methods for storing 
and maintaining the quality of food over extended periods [1, 2]. The progression of food packaging has seen notable 
advancements, transitioning from basic clay vessels to modern materials such as polymers and biopolymers [3, 4]. In the 
recent past, synthetic petrochemical-based plastics such as polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyvinylchloride (PVC), 
polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), and polyamide (PA) were increasingly used as packaging materi-
als. This was majorly due to their wider availability, low cost, and better mechanical properties such as tensile and tear 
strength, and good barrier due to their non-recyclability nature, their use at present has been restricted, as they pose 
serious ecological problems [5]. Presently, there’s a focus on cutting-edge technologies, with nanotechnology emerging 
as a promising avenue for creating innovative and highly efficient packaging solutions [6].

Nanomaterials are defined by having at least one dimension measuring between  10–9 and  10–7 m, and they are engi-
neered and utilized at an extremely small scale, boasting improved strength, chemical stability, and thermal properties 
as a result of their unique characteristics [7]. Nanomaterials find widespread applications across diverse industries.Their 
tailored properties enable precise functionality for specific applications. Despite their advantages over conventional 
materials, such as size-related benefits and versatility, nanomaterials pose certain challenges including limited data

Food packaging employing nanotechnology offers numerous advantages over traditional packaging materials by 
enhancing their various properties such as temperature resistance, durability, flame resistance, and efficient delivery of 
materials in biological systems, all cost-effectively and sustainably. Nanocomposite materials, owing to recent advance-
ments, are readily accessible, particularly to the food processing, preservation and packaging industries, including fruits 
and vegetable coatings to prolong their shelf life and delay ripening. They also play a role in extrusion and co-extrusion 
procedures in beverage production plants [7].

Innovative applications of nanomaterials are abound, e.g., the use of oxygen indicators as nano sensors in uncooked 
bacon to detect exposure to oxygen and employing carbon nanotubes with allyl isothiocyanate and cellulose as anti-
microbials in lacerated cooked chicken to impede Salmonella growth [8]. Additionally, nano clays incorporated with 
polyamide matrices lead to enhanced oxygen barrier properties, UV-blocking capability, and stiffness thereby improving 
beef packaging. [9]. Major food and beverage companies like Nestle, Kraft, Heinz, Altria, and Unilever have expressed 
interest in adopting nanotechnology to enhance the shelf life and safety of foods and beverages they manufacture 
[10, 11]. However, the safety considerations surrounding nanotechnology packaging are intricate, particularly concern-
ing the potential migration of nanomaterials into food, raising concerns about their toxicity to both humans and the 
environment. Legislation governing nanotechnology packaging varies across countries. In the United States, the Food 
and Drug Administration (FDA) regulates nanotechnology packaging in contact with food, while the European Union 
(EU) has more comprehensive regulations in this regard [12, 13]. Consequently, ensuring the safety of nanotechnology 
packaging remains a dynamic area of discussion. Further research is imperative to comprehensively evaluate the risks 
and advantages associated with the application of nanostructures in food sector. In this review, we delve into an in-depth 
examination of the evolving utilization of nanotechnology in food packaging for ensuring food safety and preservation. 
It aims to showcase recent advancements, the use of integrated technologies, and accompanying hurdles, while also 
pinpointing areas of limited understanding and suggesting avenues for further investigation in developing nanomaterial-
based towards the development of food biosafety and sustainable food packaging systems.

2   Need for nanotechnological interventions in food packaging

The prime purpose of traditional food packaging is the containment of the food material to create a barrier around the 
packaged food item against the external physical, chemical, and biological influences, and inertness of the packag-
ing material to not affect the food product. Conventional packaging materials include metal, glass, synthetic plastic, 
and paper cardboard [14], and their choice varies with the properties of the food or beverage to be packaged. Glass 
is non-reactive to most foods, a good insulator, and impermeable, and different colours of the glass could be used for 
light-sensitive food materials. Similarly, among metals, aluminum, and steel are frequently used for packaging purposes, 
especially for cans. Polymers (synthetic and non-degradable) originating from polyethylene and polypropylene, polysty-
rene, polyamide etc. are commonly used for food packaging and logistics [15]. Similarly, papers with their subtypes, kraft 
paper, sulphite paper, greaseproof paper, glassine and parchment paper, and paper boards with subtypes, white board, 
solid board, chipboard, and fibreboard, are used in food packaging as per their specialty. For example, kraft papers are 
used for packaging flours, nuts, vegetables, etc. and parchment papers are used to pack kinds of butter and fat spreads. 
Conventional packaging technologies could not address the important expectations of the conscious consumers, such 
as ensuring food safety, indicating spoilage, and longer shelf-life periods. Besides the conventional packaging materials 
and technologies, several innovations, especially nanotechnological interventions have been brought for the conveni-
ence of the consumers [16, 17]. The important innovations include the inclusion of specific compounds and technology 
for active packaging and smart packaging which is elucidated in the following section.

3   Nanotechnology‑assisted active and smart packaging systems

Selective compounds are purposefully added in active packaging to restore the nutritional value of the food and bever-
age and elongate the shelf life of the product [18]. The compound either absorbs the unwanted gases or substances 
released from the food within the package or releases desired compounds such as antioxidants, preservatives, flavour-
ings, etc. Various nanotechnological application methods have been adopted in food products. The common formats of

Intelligent packaging comprises substances/devices that can detect even minute changes in the internal environment 
of the package or product characteristics (maturity, quality, safety), and communicate such information to consumers/
stakeholders through simple, comprehensive, apparent change(s) in indicator(s) incorporated within the packaging. Thus, 
intelligent packaging does not play any role in extending shelf life or food quality, but it provides real-time quantitative 
information with respect to differences/modifications in quality attributes of the packaged food [22]. Smart sensors are 
used in the forms of time–temperature indicators, gas indicators, and shock indicators to supervise the internal conditions 
of packed foods and beverages [23]. Biopolymers are used as packaging materials in foods due to their biodegradability 
and sustainability, while natural dyes are used as pH-sensitive detectors, time–temperature indicators, carbon dioxide, 
and oxygen detectors, total volatile basic nitrogen detectors, and hydrogen sulfide detectors in the biopolymer-based 
composites act as intelligent agent(s). The application of nanomaterials has a major role in the development of intel-

ideal candidates for substituting conventional synthetic nondegradable polymers.

nanotechnology in agriculture and food are quickly expanding. Nanoparticles are employed in the food business for 
sensory enhancements, targeted nutrition and bioactive chemical delivery, active ingredient stabilization, packaging

5.1   Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs)

In comparison to organic materials, the extensive use of inorganic resources offers more benefits and promising due to 
several reasons, such as the shortcomings of organic materials like instability at high temperature and weak mechanical 
properties. The use of nanoparticles, specifically silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), is suggested as a solution to diminish these 
limitations, as they can withstand harsh processing conditions and possess antibacterial properties. The application of AgNPs 
in food packaging industries like fresh fruits, meat, seafood, and consumer products is extensive owing to their antibacterial 
properties. Several polymers have been investigated in conjunction with AgNPs for food packaging technology, and it has 
been discovered that these combinations improve the packaging’s mechanical, barrier, and antibacterial qualities as well 
as the food’s quality, shelf life, and ability to avoid spoiling [40]. More specifically, silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) can be mixed 
with edible and non-edible polymers to create active food packaging. AgNPs exhibit antibacterial, antifungal, anti-yeast, and 
antiviral properties. Because it is impossible to draw firm conclusions about the toxicity of AgNPs, food safety authorities in 
the USA and the EU regulate their actual use in food packaging cautiously. As a result, the amount of  Ag+that migrates into 
the packaged food is used to evaluate their utilization [41].

Plant-based biosynthesis of AgNPs is generally a rapid, economical, and more convenient form of synthesis as compared 
to both synthetic-based and microbial biosynthesis, as it can be useful in utilizing wastes produced by growers and han-
dlers of fruits and vegetables. Both Gram-positive and Gram-negative foodborne pathogens, as well as spoilage bacteria, 
are effectively combated by plant-mediated AgNPs. The negatively charged functional groups found in the microbial cell 
membrane bond with the silver  (Ag+) ions of AgNPs, increasing the membrane’s permeability and disrupting the cellular 
transport mechanism, resulting in cell death. Furthermore,  Ag+ ions entering the cytoplasm of a cell may harm DNA, RNA, 
peptide-forming substances, and metabolic enzymes, which could hinder microbial respiration and cell division [42].

Biopolymer packaging materials, despite their limitations such as poor mechanical qualities and moisture sensitivity, are 
being supplemented with nanoparticles, notably silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), to improve their functional properties. AgNPs 
have significant antibacterial effects against a variety of microorganisms, making them reliable in food industries for enhanc-
ing the shelf life of food goods by inhibiting microbial development. Unlike natural compounds used in edible packaging, 
which can alter the organoleptic features of food, AgNPs have no negative impact on the sensory characteristics of food 
products, making them more appealing to customers [41]. However, concerns regarding the potential migration of AgNPs 
or Ag species into the food have led food safety authorities to regulate the use of AgNPs in food packaging. To address this, 
various methods like solvent-casting and moulding methods are employed for the preparation of films attached with AgNPs, 
with the solvent-casting method being the most popular due to its relative ease of preparation [42].

5.2   Nanoclay

Both active films and coatings based on nano-clay are presently in use for enhancing the shelf life of perishable, high-moisture 
foods. The integrated nanoclays, along with bio-extracts and essential oils, can be used to fabricate nanocomposites that 
are efficient barriers, and possess antioxidant and antibacterial activities. The usage of nanoclays offers improvement in the 
mechanical, barrier, and thermal properties of films. When these nanocomposite films are combined with active agents such 
as essential oils, they exhibit antibacterial activity against foodborne pathogens, and also prevent oxidative deterioration, 
thereby extending shelf life and preserving the quality of numerous perishable food products [43, 44].

Several reports showcase about nanoclays offering a distinctive platelet design, along with flaky soft texture, low spe-
cific gravity, and a high aspect ratio, making it suitable candidate for biopackaging of various food products.. Additionally, 
different forms of nanoclays can be potentially mixed with polymers to improve their properties. Within all these nano 
clays, montmorillonite (MMT, MMT-Na+) and organophilic MMT (organic modified MMT, OMMT) have drawn interest in the 
packaging area,, since they possess a high surface area with a large aspect ratio and good compatibility with most organic 
thermoplastics [45–47].

5.4   Titanium NPs

Titanium nanoparticles (TNPs) have found widespread application in a variety of industries, including food, cosmetics, 
and electronics. TNPs have been employed in the food packaging sector to generate active packaging films by combining 
composite materials with improved functional properties. Furthermore, TNPs interact with the film matrix to boost its 
physical strength and gas barrier properties due to their antibacterial properties, which are also required for the usage 
of active food packaging. Furthermore, ethylene can be degraded by an active packaging film containing photocatalytic 
active TNPs, extending fruit shelf life after harvest. A photocatalytic system based on nano-titanium dioxide is one of the 
most effective ways to remove ethylene.

The mechanism of scavenging is based on reactive oxygen species that form on the  TiO2 surface when exposed to UV 
radiation; these species subsequently oxidize ethylene producing carbon dioxide and water. When compared to thermal 
catalytic oxidation, the titanium dioxide-based scavenging approach uses less energy and does not require high tem-
peratures or pressure. This type of scavenging system exemplifies green technology because it generates less waste and 
does not require regular replacements [51, 52]. Fresh vegetables can be stored for extended lengths of time due to the 
increased barrier properties of the  TiO2-containing active films. Fruits coated with active  TiO2 coatings lost less weight and 
decayed at a slower rate than uncoated pepper and tomato fruits, keeping superior quality throughout postharvest [53]. 
 TiO2 is a great option for a functional nanofiller that improves the performance of active food packaging films because 
of its low toxicity, economy, stability, and outstanding biocompatibility. In addition to acting as a crosslinking agent to 
enhance the film’s mechanical, water resistance, and gas barrier qualities, the addition of  TiO2 may give the active film 
antibacterial qualities. Nonetheless, the impact of  TiO2 on the characteristics of the active film is multifaceted; for instance, 
the influence of  TiO2 on the mechanical and water vapor barrier qualities of the active film is linked not only to the  TiO2 
concentration but also to the kind of film matrix and their interplay. Expanding the potential uses of  TiO2 through surface 
modification is necessary for the usage and commercialization of the functional packaging film added with  TiO2. This 
will enable  TiO2 to have photocatalytic activity under visible light, antibacterial properties, and an ability to scavenge 
ethylene even under normal storage circumstances of packaged foods like fresh fruits.  TiO2-added functional films are 
expected to be used in active food packaging applications because the addition of  TiO2 has increased the active film’s/
coating’s efficiency for food preservation. Additionally, the degree of  TiO2 movement from the active film to the food is 
negligible, and its safety has been established [54].

5.5   Nanostarch

The public’s interest in packaging that is easily recyclable, or biodegradable has grown. The next task is to improve food 
packaging’s convenience, suitability for dining out, and ecological aspects, such as by using natural polymers. Further-
more, the food’s organoleptic, nutritional, and qualitative qualities cannot be impacted using sophisticated minimal 
processing techniques. Understanding the physicochemical underpinnings of the suggested improvements is essential.

in amylopectin side chains is what gives starch its liquid-crystalline property. This architecture has recently been explained

ity, non-toxicity, and biocompatibility. Native starches are not very heat- or mechanically stable, and they are not very 
soluble or processable. They also gelatinize and retrograde easily, therefore their utility in the industry is limited.

The transformations that starch goes through include acetylation, oxidation, esterification, and hydrolysis. The acquisi-
tion of nano-starch, which is primarily comprised of two forms: starch nanoparticles (SNP) and starch nanocrystals (SNC), 
has grown in significance in recent times. The first type, called SNC crystallites, are obtained by removing the amorphous 
fraction from starch granules, usually during the acid hydrolysis process. On the other hand, the second type, called 
(SNP) crystallites, are typically spherical particles or blockets with a variable crystal structure and a range of sizes in the 
nanoscale. To convert micro-sized granules into nanometric ones, a variety of nanotechnology techniques can be used, 
such as chemical reactions (acid and enzymatic hydrolysis) and physical processes (sonication, mechanical treatments, 
or nanoprecipitation) [55].

The generation of starch nanoparticles can be performed via a variety of methods, such as hydrolysing the material 
with an acid, enzyme, or a combination of the two; regeneration; and mechanical treatments like extrusion, irradiation, 
ultrasound, or co-solvent precipitation. The simplest and most economical processes for producing starch and its deriva-
tive nanoparticles continue to be crucial. Of these techniques, ultra-sonication and nanoprecipitation are the most 
straightforward and dependable for producing the required size of nanoparticles. Ultra-sonication minimizes the dimen-
sion by violating the covalent bonds in polymeric material because of the intense shear forces or mechanical stresses 
associated with the collapsing of micro-bubbles by sound waves. The precipitation process involves dropping a diluted 
starch solution into a non-solvent one drop at a time. It is an easy, efficient, and environmentally friendly process [56].
It became apparent that the starch nanoparticles had enhanced viscosity, superior heat stability, and strong antioxi-
dant capabilities. With a greater ability to absorb water and a decreased capacity for absorbing oil, the starch nanoparti-
cles became more amorphous. These qualities might be helpful in specific medicine and food formulations, expanding 
the potential market for both the pharmaceutical and food sectors. Additionally, it was mentioned that the process for 
creating nanoparticles was easy to use, safe, and affordable, and produced better results with the appropriate particle 
size [57].

Starch-based biodegradable films are becoming increasingly popular for use in food packaging because of their 
many benefits. These include the fact that they come from plant sources (renewable resources), are free of toxins, can be 
biodegraded and biocompatible, are abundant and inexpensive, are safe to eat when used in food packaging, require 
less energy, can be disposed of in an environmentally friendly manner, and do not cause a net increase in  CO2 in the 
atmosphere. Their significant hydrophilic behaviour results in a poor moisture barrier, poor mechanical qualities, low 
water stability, high moisture sensitivity, brittleness at room temperature, and high moisture content, notwithstanding 
these positives and cons [58].

5.6   Nano‑scaled cellulose

The shelf lifespan and nutritional value of food products are greatly increased when food packaging uses nano-scaled 
cellulose [59–62]. Materials based on nanocellulose provide better moisture and oxygen barriers, avoiding spoiling and 
preserving freshness. Better food preservation is further facilitated by these material’s increased tensile strength, flex-
ibility, and decreased water vapor penetration. Furthermore, by guarding against quality changes and guaranteeing 
food safety throughout international transit, nano cellulose helps to increase the shelf life of food. Because of their high 
surface area-to-volume ratio, cellulose-based nanofibers are used in packaging to provide outstanding barrier qualities 
that successfully prevent rotting and increase the shelf life of fresh produce.

Nanocellulose allows for a significant loading of antibacterial agents. The following variables have influenced the 
incorporation of cellulose in active packaging: (1) Water stability decreases the need for organic solvents. (2) Large-scale 
surface functionalization promotes nanoparticle attachment and selective growth. (3) Facilitate the regulated introduc-
tion of bioactive components into packaged food that are encased in biopolymers. In other words, it transports anti-
oxidants, antimicrobials, and antifungal chemicals. Both chemicals and Nanocellulose are essential elements of active 
food packaging [63].

To summarize, nanocellulose has emerged as a viable material for food packaging applications due to its unique 
features, including biodegradability, non-toxicity, and high mechanical strength. It has high barrier characteristics 
against gases and water vapor, which can assist increase the shelf life of food products. Furthermore, the development

5.7   Carbon nanotubes (CNTs)

In recognition of their special qualities, carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are being utilized in food packaging techniques progres-
sively. This is how they are put into practice: (1) Enhanced Barrier Properties: CNTs can make a significant difference in 
how well-insulated packing materials are. They can serve as a barrier against biological, chemical, and physical contami-
nation, extending the product’s shelf life and preserving its quality and safety [64, 65]. Several antimicrobial properties 
of CNTs have been discovered (2), which are crucial for the preservation of food. This contributes to the food’s increased 
safety by inhibiting the growth of dangerous microorganisms. The enhancement of thermal and mechanical qualities 
(3) is associated with the application of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) in food packaging. Because of its low weight and 
good processability, the packaging is more resilient and long-lasting. Active Packaging: CNTs have the potential to be 
employed in active packaging techniques [66]. They can be used to set up an encapsulating system that releases active 
ingredients under controlled conditions. This relates more to the field of food science and technology’s development 
of innovative ingredients. (4) Environmental Impact: The trend toward more ecologically friendly products is supported 
by the usage of CNTs in food packaging. They are regarded as materials for food packaging that are safe for the environ-
ment. It is crucial to remember, nevertheless, that using CNTs comes with a number of difficulties, including processing, 
dispersion, and a substantial cost. Despite these drawbacks, CNTs present a fascinating field for study and application 
due to their possible advantages in food packaging techniques.

5.8   Nano‑silica

Owing to its special qualities, silicon dioxide  (SiO2), also known as nano silica, has found extensive application in the food 
packaging sector. Here are a few applications for it:

Enhanced Stability: To increase the stability of plastic packaging materials, nano-silica particles are coated or incor-
porated into the polymer matrix. This increases the mechanical strength and stiffness of the materials. Food safety is 
enhanced by the ability of nano-silica particles to inhibit the bacteria and viruses that cause food to deteriorate. Building 
safer food packaging is made possible by their inclusion in coatings and packaging materials.

Anti-caking Substance: Silicon dioxide  (SiO2), food additive E551, is primarily used as an anti-caking agent to increase 

the flowability of granular or powdered products, hence preventing lump formation [67, 68].

A few instances of nano silicates being employed in the food packaging sector are as follows: blueberry extracts 
have been packaged using nano-silicate. This aids in preserving the blueberries’ freshness and flavour for an extended 
amount of time.

When combined with starch, whiskers—packaging materials made from cellulose hydrolysed in an acidic solution—
have been shown to improve thermomechanical qualities, be biodegradable, and have a lower water sensitivity [69]. 
As a result, the container is stronger and more damage resistant. Plastic’s silica-NPs (SiNPs) limit gaseous exchange, 
extending the shelf life of the product [70, 71]. Due to their many advantageous properties, including their wide surface 
area, non-toxicity, biocompatibility, and absence of taste or odour, nano silica is a smart choice for applications involving 
food. Though nano-silica has several advantages for food packaging, it is crucial to remember that its proper application 
necessitates cautious thought and risk management.

5.9   Bio‑nanocomposites for packaging

Bio-nanocomposites have become a topic of extensive research and interest as they offer an interdisciplinary platform 
between biology, nanotechnology, and materials science. Bio-nanocomposites are a class of multiphase nanostructured 
materials that contain one or more constituents of biological origin and particles with at least one dimension in the 
range of 1–100 nm [72]. The aim of constructing nanocomposites is to build an advanced packaging matrix that shows 
the properties of nanocomposites like increased mechanical, barrier, thermal, and antimicrobial properties while being 
environmentally friendly [73].

Bio-nanocomposites should have dimensional stability and high mechanical strength, as the packaging material has to 
protect the food product during conditions of stress that can arise during processing, storage, handling, and distribution.

5.9.1   Nanocellulose

Nanocellulose is produced by the breakdown of cellulose fibres. The intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonds 
in cellulose make them insoluble in solvents, giving them high tensile and mechanical strength. Thus, nanocellulose 
when combined with other materials increases the thermal, mechanical, and barrier properties of the nanocompos-
ite. The formation of hydrogen bonds with the biopolymer results in a dense network with a very small pore size. This 
makes nanocellulose impermeable to gases and moisture [63]. A notable work by Bideau et al. (2018) [76] showed that 
paperboard coated with TEMPO oxidised cellulose nanofibers and polypyrrole, significantly increased the mechanical 
properties of the paperboard, which can be attributed to the presence of carboxyl group and hydrogen bonds in the 
cellulose nanofibers. Another piece of research conducted by Koppolu and colleagues showed the development of a 
nanocellulose reinforced with PLA on a paperboard. It showed a notable decrease in water vapour permeation rate by 
23% and oxygen transmission rate by 98% as compared with only PLA-coated paperboard [77].

5.9.2   Carbon nanotubes

Carbon nanomaterials have a wide number of applications in the food packaging industry. Among them, carbon nano-
tubes are defined as organic nanofillers having an ultrathin layer of carbon fibres. They can be classified as single-walled 
and multi-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs and MWCNTs) [70]. A study conducted by Yu et al. (2014) [78] demon-
strated the preparation of bio-nanocomposites of poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) consolidated 
with multi-walled carbon nanotubes that were grafted with PHBV. The uniform dispersion of the PHBV grafted MWCNTs 
in the PHBV matrix improved the mechanical stability and thermal stability of the bio-nanocomposites films at high 
temperatures, which is not present in PHBV alone. It also showed reduced water uptake necessary for food preserva-
tion. Carbon nanotubes are known to show antimicrobial properties, which can be incorporated into food packaging 
applications. Wen et al. (2020) performed a study to analyze poly (vinyl alcohol) (PVA) nanocomposites reinforced with 
zinc-oxide doped MWCNTs (MWCNTs-ZnO). Zinc oxide plays a key role as an antibacterial agent. The antibacterial abil-
ity of the nanocomposite film was tested against Escherichia coli for 24 h and it showed inhibition of bacterial growth

layer nanoclay having a hollow tubular structure, with improved physical and mechanical stability, optical, thermal, and 
rheological characteristics [80]. A recent piece of article, demonstrates a composite using natural halloysite nanotube as

enhanced free radical scavenging activity, antibacterial properties, and pH-sensitive performance [81].

6   Engineered nanomaterials for effective food packaging and preservation

The development of nanoparticle-based packaging materials has proven advantageous in the food and beverage 
industry. Application of nanoparticle-based packaging materials in the food industry remains limited due to the risk of 
food getting contaminated with nanoparticles which may lead to human oral toxicity [87]. But, with the emergence of 
engineered nanomaterials in food packaging, active and intelligent attributes have been added. The major advantage 
of using engineered nanoparticles to develop packaging materials is to enhance their mechanical, thermal, and anti-
microbial properties [88]. Further, in vivo human toxicity studies have also shown that engineered nanoparticles were 
clinically safe if taken orally [89]. Due to this reason, a broad range of engineered nanomaterials are being developed and 
explored for their possible use in primary food packaging as food contact materials (FCMs). Engineered nanoparticles 
can be derived from metal or non-metal nanoparticles. Amongst them, nanoengineered materials having antimicrobial 
capabilities have been widely used in packaging in order to increase the shelf-life of packaged foods. Nanomaterials 
incorporated with metal nanoparticles like silver (Ag), gold (Au), Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn), Palladium (Pd), Platinum (Pt), and 
Selenium (Se) are some of the widely evaluated due to their antimicrobial properties [89]. Apart from these, metal oxide 
nanoparticles like titanium dioxide  (TiO2), zinc oxide (ZnO), calcium oxide (CaO), magnesium oxide (MgO), aluminium 
oxide  (Al2O3), and cerium oxide  (CeO2) have also gathered attention as antimicrobial agents in packaging due to their 
ability to absorb UV and for possessing photocatalytic disinfecting abilities [90, 91]. Apart from these, engineered nano-
particles derived from non-meals like clay and organic materials like protein, polymers, chitosan, and poly-lactic acid 
have also found their way into the food packaging industry. Nanoclay has been incorporated into polymers in order to 
increase their strength, thermal resistance and stability [92]. Nanoparticles derived from organic materials like chitosan 
incorporates antimicrobial properties into polymer food packaging [93]. Although the use of engineered nanoparticles 
has increased in packaging, it is still being hindered by the skepticism surrounding its toxicity and bioaccumulation. In 
order to accept their use in the food industry, engineered nanoparticles must be stringently evaluated by human risk 
assessment studies. So far, we have very few studies that have evaluated human exposure and assessment models for

7   Green synthesis of nanomaterials for food packaging

Recently, green synthesis of nanomaterials has gained extensive attention primarily due to its eco-friendly approaches 
and cost-effectiveness. Green synthesis involves both plant or microbial products stabilizing agents or reducing 
agents (Table 3). Nanoparticles synthesized via green technology exhibit higher stability and appropriate dimensions, 
specializing them as an ideal candidate for smart and active food packaging mainly due to mechanical, thermal, and 
biodegradable properties. Extensive studies unveil that nanostructured materials are widely employed in industries 
including technology, medical, and food sector [97]. As compared to conventional physical and chemical methods 
[98] for the synthesis of nanomaterials, biological or green methods significantly expense less energy consumption 
and have zero impact on the environment and human health. Green synthesis techniques use bio-resources avail-
able in nature including diversified microbes, plant extracts, and bioactive compounds that minimize hazardous 
by-products (Fig. 3).

Consequently, due to the expanding global population and industrialization, the demand for more healthy foods 
with increased shelf life has been growing. Amongst several, food packaging is highlighted as one of the major 
aspects of food industries that play a key role in fulfilling the demands of the customers and maintaining food nutri-
tional value and quality [99]. Green synthesis has emerged as a stimulating and promising approach that ensures 
sustainable alternatives to various chemical-based technologies without compromising the quality, safety, and nutri-
tional value of food products [100]. Nanomaterials production through a green route may likely include microbes, 
plant, plant components like leaf, flower, peel, etc., or metabolites such as proteins, vitamins, polysaccharides, phe-
nols, flavonoids as an eco-friendly, and non-toxic machinery to overcome the detrimental ecological impacts asso-
ciated with conventional methods [101, 102]. Likewise, green synthesis mediated by microorganisms has acquired 
a specific advantage due to their high growth rate, ease of cultivation, and ability to grow in ambient conditions of 
temperature, pH, and pressure [103]. A diversity of microorganisms including bacterial and fungal sp. can serve as 
potential biofactories for inexpensive synthesis of various nanomaterials containing metals such as zinc, copper, 
silver, gold silver, titanium, palladium, and nickel [104] that exhibit a sustainable approach in smart and active food 
packaging industries.

8   Conclusion and future prospects

For years, synthetic polymeric materials have remained the predominant source of food packaging. Biopolymers have 
many desirable characteristics like biodegradability, eco-friendliness, renewability, nontoxicity, and lightweight, mak-
ing them an ideal choice for food packaging applications. However, pure biopolymers have properties like expensive, 
lower mechanical barrier, and thermal properties which are hindering their applications in the food industry. Nanoma-
